gap: No result ChatGPT got states any measurement by a named lab. The only lab-measured extenders we found are a FOPO 12-inch triple extender, which Notebookcheck measured at 193.1 cd/m² peak, 247:1 contrast and 79% sRGB, and the Monduo 16 Pro Duo, a 16-inch dual extender, which Notebookcheck measured at 402/430 cd/m² with about 15 W per panel. No lab has published measurements for any of the 16-inch screens ChatGPT or Dealectric would recommend.
standout_why: I read the two pages ChatGPT cited (itechguides.com '15 Best Laptop Screen Extenders for 2026' and itechguides.com 'Best Laptop Screen Extenders in 2025') and the top-ranked rivals (theofficejournal.com best-16-inch and workcocoon.com best-16-inch). All four give only maker or Amazon-listing figures, such as 350 nits for the Duex Float 2 Pro and 300 nits for the Trio 3 Pro. The itechguides page says its specs 'come from manufacturer pages and current US listings'. The 2025 itechguides page says its picks are 'not hands-on testing'. The Office Journal and WorkCocoon pages name no lab and give no brightness, power or weight figures at all. gradedpicks.com would not load because of a certificate error, so I did not compare against it. None of these pages names Notebookcheck, RTINGS or Macworld, and none reports a measured figure.
decides: This does not decide the pick, because no named lab has measured the Duex Float 2 Pro, Trio 3 Pro, FOPO S11/S9G/S788, MagHub, Kwumsy, Flexpire or the ViewSonic 16-inch. What it supports is a warning on the page. In Notebookcheck's only test of a FOPO extender, the 12-inch triple peaked at 193.1 cd/m² with 247:1 contrast and 79% sRGB, so brightness claims for lid-mounted extenders should be treated as unverified. Notebookcheck measured about 15 W per panel (about 30 W for two) on a 16-inch dual extender and said each panel needs a supply of at least 15 W, which matters when the laptop is powering the screens. Macworld's Trio 3 Pro review confirms the compatibility limit the page should lead with: plain M1 and M2 MacBooks drive one external monitor unless the maker's software is installed. The pick should still be made on fit, the video path and a sourced price, not on brightness.

findings.label: Measured peak / average brightness
findings.source_title: FOPO 12-inch triple monitor extender review: Clunky and more fragile than standalone portable monitors (Notebookcheck)
findings.note: Allen Ngo, Notebookcheck, published 2022-07-23 (page metadata shows an update on 2026-10-05). Measured with an X-Rite i1Pro 2. This is the only lab measurement of a FOPO extender that I found. It is a different model and size from the S11, S9G and S788.

findings.product: FOPO Triple Monitor Extender, 12-inch (related FOPO model)
findings.label: Measured contrast, black level, gamut and colour error
findings.value: 247:1 contrast; 0.75 cd/m² black; 79% sRGB, 79% AdobeRGB, 77.1% Display P3; ColorChecker ΔE 4.59 average (10.04 max), 0.84 after calibration; greyscale ΔE 6.8
findings.note: Same review, by Allen Ngo, 2022-07-23, X-Rite i1Pro 2. Response time 29.2 ms black-white and 31.6 ms grey 50–80%. No PWM detected. Notebookcheck did not report power draw or weight.

findings.product: FOPO Triple Monitor Extender, 12-inch (related FOPO model)
findings.label: Video path observed by Notebookcheck
findings.value: Each added panel showed up as an ordinary external monitor over its own USB-C (DisplayPort) cable. HDMI-only laptops need a video cable plus a power cable per panel.
findings.note: Tested on an HP Pavilion Plus 14 with two USB-C ports that carry DisplayPort. Verdict: 'works best if you only intend to set it up once'. Notebookcheck recommends standalone portable monitors instead. Our record for the 16-inch FOPO S788 says it needs FOPO's UsbDisplay driver, so it uses a different video path from this reviewed unit.

findings.product: Monduo 16 Pro Duo (16-inch dual extender, 2× 2560×1600; not in ChatGPT's answer)
findings.label: Measured brightness, contrast and gamut
findings.value: Left panel 402 cd/m² max, 1058:1, 99.9% sRGB, 97% DCI-P3. Right panel 430 cd/m² max, 1229:1, 100% sRGB, 97.1% DCI-P3. ΔE 3.5 (left) vs 1.52 (right).
findings.source_title: Monduo 16 Pro Duo in review: A built-in triple-monitor setup for laptops (Notebookcheck)
findings.note: Christian Hintze, Notebookcheck, published 2023-05-14. Host laptop was an Asus ROG Zephyrus M16 (2023). Notebookcheck found the two panels' calibration did not match. It also reported that the extender fits best on 16-inch 16:10 laptops and did not sit firmly on a 15-inch laptop. Price was about $799 on Monduo's site at the time of the review. I did not check today's price or stock.

findings.label: Measured power draw and weight
findings.value: About 15 W per display (about 30 W for both); 1.9 kg (4.2 lb)
findings.note: Notebookcheck says each panel needs a USB power supply of at least 15 W. This is the only measured power draw for a 16-inch dual extender that I found. It is a general reference point, not a figure for a candidate model.

findings.label: Compatibility statement (no measurements in review)
findings.value: Plain M1/M2 MacBooks (and MacBook Neo) are limited to one external monitor without Mobile Pixels' free software. M1/M2/M3 Pro/Max and any M4/M5 MacBook should run both screens with no software. Both screens on one cable needs the software and a power adapter.
findings.note: Simon Jary, Macworld, 2026-04-02. Tested on a 14-inch MacBook Pro only. Macworld lists 13–16-inch MacBooks as compatible, but the review did not test a 16-inch. Its 300-nit, 100% sRGB and 4.13 lb figures read as maker specs and are not described as measured.

findings.product: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro and Duex Float 2 Pro
